title: The path to the button
instruction: The nodes are screens of the class app; the edges are the transitions between them. The number on an edge says how many seconds the transition takes: tapping, searching with your eyes, typing and waiting for the server. Find the user’s fastest path to the goal.

levels.story: Ondra wants to pay for the trip. What is the fastest way to the Pay button?
levels.why: Home → Menu → Payments → Pay takes 6 s. The Trips tile right on the home screen is only one tap, but it’s hidden at the bottom and you spend 6 s looking for it. Close doesn’t mean fast.

levels.story: The app sent a notification, “Pay for the trip!”. Tapping it opens a website where you have to log in again. Is the shortcut really a shortcut?
levels.why: The path through the notification has only two taps, but it takes 10 s because of logging in again. The fastest is Home → Menu → Payments → Pay in 6 s, even though it has three taps. The number of taps isn’t the only thing the user feels.

levels.story: The teacher needs to find out whether Ondra has paid. Find the fastest path to the Payment status screen.
levels.why: Home → Menu → Payments → Payment status takes 7 s: Payments has an “Unpaid” filter and Ondra is visible straight away. The path through Ondra’s profile makes human sense (“I’m looking for a person”), but it takes 9 s. Good navigation leads to the question the user is trying to answer, not to the place where the data lives.

debrief: Designers measure a user’s path in time, not just in taps. Searching with your eyes, typing and waiting for the server count too. When you time the main task in your own app with a stopwatch, you’ll see where a shortcut helps and where it only looks good.
